title: Your Kidneys Filter 180 Litres a Day. Why Don't You Pee It?
description:
How do your kidneys work? About a million tiny filters called nephrons in each kidney sieve around 180 litres of fluid a day, then take back about 99 percent of it, so only 1 to 2 litres leaves as urine.

topic: Your Kidneys Explained in Simple Words: how they clean all your blood
script: Your kidneys filter 180 litres a day, so why don't you pee 180 litres? That's like 180 big bottles of water, every single day. And each kidney is only about the size of your fist. So how do two little beans wash all of your blood, and still know exactly what to keep? Let's go inside. First, where are they? Not down low where most people point. Your kidneys sit high up in your back, tucked under your bottom ribs, one on each side. Each one weighs about 150 grams, about as much as a smartphone. But they're hungry for blood. Around one fifth of everything your heart pumps, goes straight to your kidneys. That's about a litre of blood, every minute. So over a day, your blood passes through them again and again. Now let's zoom in. Each kidney is packed with about a million tiny filters, called nephrons. And every nephron starts with a little ball of blood vessels, called the glomerulus. Think of it like a coffee filter made of blood vessels. Or a kitchen sieve that lets the water through but keeps the pasta. Blood squeezes through it under pressure. Water, salt, sugar and waste slip through the thin walls. But big things, like blood cells and proteins, are too large, so they stay in the blood. That liquid that slips through is called filtrate. And this is where those 180 litres come from. But wait. If you peed out 180 litres a day, you'd be in the bathroom nonstop. So here's the clever part. The filtrate flows down a long, twisty tube. And along the way, the tube grabs back almost everything useful. Sugar, back into the blood. Most of the salt, back into the blood. And water, back into the blood. In fact, about 99 percent of the filtrate gets reabsorbed. What's left is mostly extra water and waste, like urea, a leftover from breaking down protein. That's your urine. Only about one to two litres a day. So out of 180 litres filtered, you keep almost all of it. That's some serious recycling. It drips down a tube called the ureter, into your bladder, and waits there until you're ready to go. So the kidneys don't just throw out the trash. They pick the treasure back out of it. And cleaning is only half the job. Your kidneys also keep your water balanced. Drink a lot, and they let more water go. Get thirsty, and they hold on to it. That's why your pee changes color during the day. They also make chemical messengers. One, called renin, helps control your blood pressure. Another, called EPO, tells your bone marrow to make more red blood cells. And they turn vitamin D into its active form, which helps keep your bones strong. They even keep your blood from getting too acidic, and when your blood sugar runs low, they can make a little sugar of their own. So a million filters, a litre of blood a minute, and 180 litres cleaned every day, all from two organs the size of your fist. Pretty amazing for something you never even feel working. Next time, why do you have two nostrils, and why is one always more blocked?
key_facts: Each kidney has about a million nephrons (KCUK)
Kidneys filter roughly 180 L of fluid a day (Lumen: ~180 L/day men, ~150 L/day women; KCUK says ~200 L)
About 99 percent of the filtrate is reabsorbed; 1-2 L of urine a day
About 20 percent of the heart's output, roughly 1 L of blood per minute, goes to the kidneys
Each kidney is about fist-sized and about 150 g
Glomerulus: cluster of tiny blood vessels whose thin walls let water, salts, wastes through; blood cells and large proteins stay
Kidneys release renin (blood pressure), EPO (red blood cells), activate vitamin D, balance water and acid, and can make glucose
